en: We endured a dog’s humiliation,
The enormity of grievous disgrace.
Will this accursed swine never mend?
Can the world not sate him?
Will he keep this nation beneath a cloud of dust
Until he has slaughtered them all together?
Under Sarybai’s venom,
Under the calamity of his wrath,
Countless armies of the people died;
Everyone old enough to know reason died.
The infidel’s fury mounted,
And he stirred a savage battle;
His wrath rose time and again.
Great hosts, sparing no blood,
Clashed and fought,
While I, in black mourning veil,
Amid the bloodshed of battle,
Stand locked in combat.
If my strength allows, I shall strike
That troublesome swine,
And lay him on his back;
I shall drag him along the road,
And defeat him if he comes to battle;
I shall drink like liquor the blood
Of that invincible boar.
If death seizes me and my day ends,
I shall yield my precious life.
Against that fierce swine of a foe
I shall try my strength in combat!
When fate arrives, must one not die?
Must not every mortal born
Meet the Creator’s decree?
When the naked taker of souls,
Who reaches out amid the strife,
Draws near,
The speaking tongue is stilled—
What soul can escape?
Subduing the whole wide world,
The black earth, barren of fat—
“Do not grieve, my people,”
Said Sarybay, son of the ogre.
His white-barreled gun was enormous;
Nothing like it existed in the world.
As they advanced to meet,
They fell upon each other with war cries;
Before countless gathered peoples,
Such was the shape of this conflict,
Such was the venom the accursed one spoke.
This was the fate of the city-dwelling folk:
From Sarybay’s venom,
From the violence of his wrath,
Unable to endure his oppression,
The noble, wealthy people
Burned and smoldered into embers.
The red-necked falcons,
Champions surpassing ordinary men,
Vanished entirely from among my people.
Many warriors fought;
Then at one fateful time
He made widows of those with husbands,
And drove living people into slavery.
Not once, but a thousand times he did it.
He leveled hills into plains,
And used force against noble heads.
He bound and ruined much of my fortune,
And shattered many of my hopes;
He made my people groan
And utterly broke my back.
Hear my truthful words:
You have waged war many times,
And still I have not taken my revenge.
Among round-headed mortals,
Among peoples armed with every weapon,
His doom is hell and his venom strong;
No horror like this exists.
When he rode out from Zhelpinish,
He came leading ten thousand troops,
Driving the entire host together;
When they saw wild rams, they chased and ate them,
When they saw argali, they shot and ate them,
When they saw ibex, they gathered and ate them—
Every living soul suffered there.
Their heads ensnared in torment,
He shot and destroyed them all.
He came to exterminate
The Kyrgyz line to its very root,
Saying, “I shall sweep them all away.”
These were Khan Seytek’s words.
Sarybay came forth to face him;
Such were the heroes.
Wrapped in blue, bullet-proof armor,
Raging like a gray-blue tiger,
That infidel Sarybay cried:
“Wretched Seytek,
If a host comes crowding behind you,
And overwhelms your precious life,
You shall see in the blink of an eye
How readily you turn back!
You will see such calamity;
You call yourself a lion born of heroes!”
Then, poised like a black eagle,
Raging in fury,
Khan Sarybay stood there,
Appearing like a colossal giant.
Before he could turn his horse’s mouth,
When the madman flew into rage,
While Khan Sarybay stood there,
No man dared face him,
No mortal could approach him.
He thundered like a mountain,
Mustering courage in his grim wrath,
And when he loomed before them,
The great host split ten ways.
Eagerly bracing himself,
Swaying with menace,
Sparks flew from his mace,
Fire streamed from his fury,
Blood issued from his black eyes,
And death breathed from his menace.
Glowering wrathfully,
With a black purse at his belt,
His voice made the space
Between earth and blue sky tremble.
His surpassing courage surged,
All his might was in his hands;
As though devouring mankind,
He darkened and scowled,
Spitting blood and chewing stones.
His deeds were those of a tiger;
Such was his looming form.
Unhurried, unflustered, unconcerned,
This scion of a mighty people
Had been endowed beyond measure
By Almighty God the Creator.
Sarybay, son of the ogre,
Was a sight for mortals to behold;
Any mortal who encountered
His appearance and form
Might die before his appointed death—
Such was his aspect.
And if you looked at the man himself,
He resembled the naked taker of souls.
He was tall as a plane tree;
At the villain’s appearance
No man could stand unmoved.
He charged like a boar,
And pursued like the wind;
The way he faced his foe
Was like a bolt of lightning.
His strength was fearsome, his venom fierce;
Such was the one who matched him.
He gnawed whoever crossed his path,
And seemed ready to take the life of any challenger;
Such was he when his measure was taken.
Then Sarybay
Raised his steel-bladed Zulfiqar,
A mighty weapon that shattered combat.
When one whose true death had arrived
Fell afoul of the wrathful man,
Sarybay’s sweeping arm
Brought down foes too heavy for horses;
On every field where he fought,
He was manifestly swift and skillful.
The wisest and strongest,
All who entered
The fury of the melee—
Even those renowned throughout the world—
He shattered countless lives,
Leaving them strewn one by one.
The ill-fated brute
Had raised a great storm of battle.
Sarybay was such a lion,
Meeting assembled champions
And standing amid their war cries,
Where heads were hewn off and blood was shed;
He was the lion who strode onto the field.
Striking like a young tiger,
Such was the host that fought and shattered.
The mighty battle raised a tremendous din,
A tumult of ringing war cries.
Against the ranks, vast as Mount Kap,
Against the warrior Khan Sarybay,
He crashed like a thundering mountain,
Rushing to destroy the people
And overrun the whole wide world.
This descendant of a noble lion,
Who never shrank from death,
Was not Sarybay but one man against countless hosts;
Your forefather never retreated.
He rejoiced when told of joy
And burned when told of death;
Told to drink water, he drank poison;
Told to take a cap, he cut off a head;
Told to spill blood, he poured out lives.
He was the offspring of a renowned lion—
Such, I see, was Seytek.
His first forefather had been a khan,
And the forty Chinese tribes had dwelt at ease.
He began the shooting and stirred conflict,
Never pausing to heed any man;
Unable to withstand his courage,
The peoples of the whole world were laid waste—
So the impassioned warrior Seytek
Waited and took his turn,
While his bitter foes fell still.
The noble lion’s descendant
Turned the head of his gray kulan steed
And leveled Manas the lion’s ornamented spear,
Making it thunder as he thrust.
Sarybay was his opponent,
Who had wrought such calamity;
Pouring out his wrath, Seytek shouted
And invoked the sacred spirit
Of Manas, his royal forefather.
He broke through forest and mountain to clear a road
And set his hand to a mountain-sized deed;
His battle cry deafened the ears.
He invoked the spirits of his ancestors
And of the many heroes of former cities,
Calling upon their sacred power,
And Seytek leveled his spear.
Sarybay, son of the ogre,
Knew well his own great strength
And now smiled beneath his mustache:
“I shall snuff out his burning lamp
And send him from this world;
I shall beat the fierce spirit from him.
Now I shall settle his account,
Make the boy scream,
And cut short his fly-sized soul.
I shall wreak boundless ruin
And take as spoil Kulansur,
The steed no bullet can catch.
The brute has run mad;
I shall soak his body in blood
And lay him down to grease the earth.
When he comes near, I shall cut off his head
And crush his liver like sausage.
This swine seeking blood
Has come to me himself,” he said.
“The raging champion’s time
To be slain here
Has now arrived,” he said.
“This young fool doomed to death,
This rabid cur,
Has come here himself,” he said.
“I shall roast him like wheat;
From this cur of a champion
I shall tear out the great artery of his head.
This wounded conqueror of foes—
I shall kill him and cut off his head,
And pierce his eyes, bright as Venus.
I shall unleash a mighty battle;
